title: How Did He Do It?
plain_title: What the fiscal 2027 executive budget does and does not fix
what_they_audited: A Citizens Budget Commission report analyzing Mayor Zohran Mamdani's fiscal year 2027 executive budget for New York City.
background: The budget is balanced, as the law requires, and it corrects years of underbudgeting to give a fuller picture of the city's spending obligations.

findings.plain: Most of the actions used to balance the fiscal 2026 and 2027 budgets do not stabilize the budget over the long run, including one-shot resources and delayed payments.
findings.quote: Sixty-one percent of the budget balancing actions over fiscal years 2026 and 2027 do nothing to stabilize the budget long term

findings.plain: Projected gaps in later years grow, before accounting for employee raises or new programs.
findings.quote: Projected budget gaps grow from $7.1 billion in fiscal year 2028 to $9.8 billion in fiscal year 2030

findings.plain: Stretching out pension contributions lowers payments in the near term but raises them substantially in the 2030s.
findings.quote: It lowers contributions $10.7 billion through fiscal year 2032 but adds $15.6 billion in new contributions from fiscal years 2033 through 2037.

findings.plain: The savings program under Executive Order 12 produces savings over two years, but only about a quarter of the initiatives increase efficiency.
findings.quote: Executive Order 12 initiatives save $1.8 billion over two years, but only 26 percent increase efficiency.

findings.plain: Delaying the state class size reduction mandate saves money now but leaves an annual cost later.
findings.quote: Delaying the Class Size Reduction mandate saves money for now, but leaves the City to ultimately spend $1.4 billion annually

findings.plain: City headcount rises on net, as new positions outnumber eliminated vacancies.
findings.quote: The budget increases headcount by 869 full-time positions, with the elimination of 2,268 vacancies offset by 3,137 new positions

findings.plain: The budget adds new spending, part of it for administration priorities such as housing production and childcare and the rest to support existing programs.
findings.quote: Fully $3.5 billion in newly added spending includes $1.3 billion for administration priorities such as housing production and childcare

recommendations: Double the Executive Order 12 savings initiatives to $2 billion in fiscal year 2027 and increase them by $1 billion each year after that.
Take further steps to cut costs in fast-growing areas including CityFHEPS housing vouchers and special education due process (Carter) cases.
Pay for additional new spending and City Council initiatives with recurring savings.
Raise the fiscal year 2027 general reserve to $500 million.
